title: Honeypot
summary: A honeypot is a decoy system, service, account or file with no legitimate production purpose, placed where it should not be touched, so that any interaction is suspicious by construction and produces high-signal, low-noise detection. Honeypots range from a single exposed port that simply records connection attempts and submitted credentials, through emulated services inside the network that detect lateral movement, to full research environments used to study attacker tooling and families of malware. Their value to defenders is early warning of scanning, exploitation attempts and internal reconnaissance that endpoint agents and perimeter logs may miss, plus a small amount of attacker time consumed on a worthless target. The mistake is deploying a decoy with a real hostname, reused credentials or weak isolation, so it becomes a stepping stone rather than a trap, or treating every contact as a confirmed breach when scanners, backup jobs and misconfigured applications can also touch it. Alerts from a decoy are leads that require the same context and triage as any other detection.

beginner.definition: A honeypot is a fake system that is meant to be attacked. It has no real job, so nobody honest should ever touch it. When someone does touch it, you know something is wrong. Security teams watch the honeypot and learn how the intruder behaves.
beginner.whyItMatters: Real networks produce so many alerts that important ones get lost. A honeypot produces very few alerts, because almost every contact with it is suspicious. It can warn you early that someone is exploring your network. It can also slow an intruder down, because they waste time on a system that holds nothing. Without decoys, you may learn about an intrusion only after data has left.
howItWorks: You place a fake service or file where real data should never be.
The decoy records every connection, command and login attempt that reaches it.
Alerts go straight to the security team, because normal users never connect.
The team blocks the source and then looks for the same behaviour elsewhere.
The decoy sits in its own network segment, kept away from real servers.
Operators review those logs later to learn which tools and tricks were used.
beginner.example: Imagine a shop that leaves an empty till near the door. Honest customers walk past it and pay at the real counter. A thief goes straight to the empty till, and the camera sees everything. The shop learns when and how the thief works, and loses nothing of value. The trick is to make the till look real and to keep it far from the safe. A honeypot works in exactly that way for a network.
takeaways: A honeypot has no real purpose, so any contact with it is worth investigating.
Keep decoys isolated, because an attacker may try to use one as a step inward.
Treat a honeypot hit as a lead, not as proof, and check your own tools too.

objectives: Explain what a honeypot is and why its alerts carry unusually high signal.
Distinguish research honeypots from production decoys used for early warning.
Describe how a decoy is isolated, monitored and kept safe to operate.
Explain what honeypot logs teach a defensive team about attacker behaviour.
Name the legal, privacy and safety checks to complete before deploying a decoy.
